title: Nothing shall separate (Romans 8:35–39)
hook: neither death nor life nor angels nor height nor depth

segments.voice: Yesterday, sunergei, and not the greeting-card version. Your line was all things.

Make a list of the things you're most afraid of. Be honest. Losing someone. Getting sick. Being alone. Money running out. Something you did coming to light. Dying. Most people carry a list like that somewhere below the surface, and it gets louder at night. Paul made one too, at the end of Romans 8. Then he did something unexpected with it. He put the word nothing in front of it.
screen: `A LIST OF YOUR FEARS.` → `PAUL MADE ONE TOO.` → `THEN HE WROTE: NOTHING.`

segments.voice: First the question, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation? or distress? or famine? or nakedness? or danger? or persecution? or the sword?" Not abstractions for Paul. He'd been shipwrecked, beaten with rods, hungry, cold, in danger from rivers and robbers, and tradition says he'd die by the sword in Rome. Then: "But in all these things we overcome, because of him that hath loved us." And the great list: "For I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor might, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." He builds it mostly in pairs: death and life, angels and principalities, things present and things to come, height and depth. Every moment of time, every corner of space, every power seen and unseen. And in case he missed something: nor any other creature. I am sure, he says. Not I hope. Convinced. Notice what he doesn't promise. He doesn't say none of these things will happen. He says none of them can cut the thread between you and the love of God. The Church reads this passage at many funerals, because it reaches even past death. And it ends the great chapter that began with no condemnation. From no condemnation to no separation.
screen: `WHO SHALL SEPARATE US?` · `IN ALL THESE THINGS WE OVERCOME.` · `NEITHER DEATH, NOR LIFE, NOR HEIGHT.` · `NOR ANY OTHER CREATURE.` · then, large: `NOTHING SHALL SEPARATE US.`

segments.voice: Pick one fear and say it to yourself plainly, losing my job, my diagnosis, my kid's future, and in the same breath add Paul's words: nothing shall separate us. Not a spell that makes the fear go away, just a sentence set beside it. If you pray, rest in the love of God that Paul was sure of; if not, notice what it's like to set a fear beside a promise.
Separate. The Greek word behind Paul's great list: nothing in time or space can separate us from the love of God. Today's word.

Your line: nothing shall separate us. And that's week eighty-one: justification, poured, buried with him, wretched, the Spirit prays, sunergei, and nothing shall separate. Day five hundred sixty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Romans 8:31–39 is one of the readings the Church offers for Catholic funeral Masses, and many Catholics keep these verses close in illness and grief.

fork.setup: you're Paul, listing every danger you can think of. what do you do with the list?
options: promise none of it will happen.
say none of it can separate us from God's love.
tell people not to think about it.
fork.reveal: he puts nothing in front of the whole list: neither death, nor life, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us.

original.note: Greek: to separate, divide, put apart. nothing shall be able to separate us.

trapdoor: what you thought: a comforting verse for hard times.
what it means: Paul names every power of time, space and creation, and says none can cut us off from the love of God in Christ.
what a scholar hears: height and depth may echo astrological terms for the heavens, which ancient people feared ruled their fate. Paul places even these under nothing.

chat.says: When something terrible happens, does it mean God has stopped loving us?
options: Paul lists every fear, even death, and says nothing can separate us from God's love.
Paul says God's love holds through this life, but death is where it ends.
Paul promises that those who love God will be spared famine or danger.
chat.meaning: Paul doesn't promise hard things won't happen; he's sure nothing in time or space, not even death, can separate us from God's love.

principalities.meaning: an old word for ruling powers, seen or unseen

persecution.meaning: being hunted or punished for your faith

Douay-Rheims.meaning: the old Catholic English translation of the Bible

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of Romans 8:35, 8:37 and 8:38–39 (Douay has 'I am sure' and adds 'nor might').
Romans 8:31b–35, 37–39 in the Order of Christian Funerals readings: confirm.
Paul's death by the sword is tradition, not scripture; the script says so in the myth. Confirm.
Height and depth (hypsōma, bathos) as possible astrological terms: a scholarly suggestion, hedged; confirm.
